rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period demand payment
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 notice drawer within thirty days
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 cause of action complaint limitation
rows.answer:
The notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint is fifteen days of the receipt of the notice demanding payment, as provided under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, according to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The payee or the holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice, as stated in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 covers cognizance of offences and requires the complaint to be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 [8].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to consideration for negotiable instruments
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
rows.answer:
Until the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated, or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. As explained in the Supreme Court judgment in K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr., this presumption imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption in favour of the holder that the instrument was made for consideration, thereby shifting the burden of proof to the defendant to establish that the promissory note is not supported by consideration [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails [2].
- Section 58 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which covers an instrument obtained by unlawful means or for unlawful consideration [3].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
coercion undue influence fraud misrepresentation voidable contracts consent
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion definition
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1] [2]. However, such a contract is not voidable if the consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence and the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as provided in the exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, a fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party does not render the contract voidable under the explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 14 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines "Free consent" as consent not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake [3].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
capacity of parties to contract unsound mind minor
topSources: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 sO32
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, stating that "All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void" [7].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder capital offense life imprisonment death penalty
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. [1]

Related provisions:
- Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, on "Punishment for murder by life-convict", stating that whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life [2].
- Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, on "Murder", defining when culpable homicide is murder [6].
- Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, on "Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder" [3].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
theft punishment Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft
Indian Penal Code section 379 theft
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
rows.answer:
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, under sub-section (2) of Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1] (previously Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860) [9]. For a second or subsequent conviction, the punishment shall be rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and up to five years, along with fine [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- For first-time convictions of theft where the stolen property's value is less than five thousand rupees, upon returning the property's value or restoring the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft in a dwelling house, transport, place of worship, or government property, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [3].
- Section 306 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft by a clerk or servant of property in master's possession, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [5].

rows.question: What is the punishment for defamation?
queries: What is the punishment for defamation?

topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531

rows.answer:
Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1] (which replaced Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [9]).

Related provisions:
- Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers the printing or engraving of matter, knowing or having good reason to believe it is defamatory, with punishment up to two years simple imprisonment, fine, or both [1].
- Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 also covers the sale or offering for sale of any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing it contains such matter, with punishment up to two years simple imprisonment, fine, or both [1].
- Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers the prosecution for defamation, requiring a complaint by an aggrieved person or, under specific circumstances or for public servants, a complaint by the Public Prosecutor before a Court of Session [5].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
queries: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?
person accused of non bailable offence release on bail conditions
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita section 480 bail in case of non bailable offence
Code of Criminal Procedure section 437 bail in non bailable cases
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s480
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s482
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s478
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
rows.answer:
A person accused or suspected of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by an officer in charge of a police station or by a court other than the High Court or Court of Session, unless there appear reasonable grounds for believing that they have been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or unless they are barred due to previous convictions as specified, though courts may direct release for children, women, the sick or infirm, or for other special reasons under Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [1] (previously Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [9]).

Conditions and time limits:
- The person must execute a bond for their appearance [1].
- If released under sub-section (1) for an offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more or under Chapter VI, Chapter VII, or Chapter XVII of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the court must impose conditions that the person shall attend in accordance with the bond, shall not commit a similar offence, and shall not directly or indirectly make any inducement, threat, or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case or tamper with evidence [1]

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s58

rows.answer:
A sale is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, according to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [2]. 

In order to constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another where all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, as discussed in the Supreme Court judgment "Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others" [11].

Regarding how a sale is completed and made:
- In the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, a transfer can be made only by a registered instrument, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [2].
- In the case of tangible immovable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, the transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [2].

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?

rows.answer:
The punishment for identity theft using a electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to rupees one lakh under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which covers punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource [5].
